result.summary: A set of quoted fragments from the lost Great Eoiae, a catalogue-style poem of heroines and heroes. They record genealogies, myths of Heracles, Melampus, Phineus and Endymion, and the story of Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle and turning Battus to stone.

scenes.title: Genealogy fragments
scenes.summary: Short citations give the descent and marriages of Argive and Boeotian figures, including Epidaurus, Thero, Mecionice, Hyettus, Peirene and Mycene.

scenes.title: Suitors killed by Oenomaus
scenes.summary: The poem lists the suitors of Hippodamia who were killed by Oenomaus in the chariot race.
scenes.stakes: Suitors risk death in the race.

scenes.title: Endymion, Melampus, Scylla, Phineus
scenes.summary: Endymion is cast down to Hades for desiring Hera. Melampus gains prophecy from a serpent's young and escapes Iphiclus. Scylla's parentage and Phineus' blinding are noted.
scenes.stakes: Melampus is bound and faces death in a collapsing house.

scenes.title: Children of Phrixus
scenes.summary: Four sons of Phrixus and Iophossa are named, and the descent of Magnes is given.

scenes.title: Hermes steals cattle; Battus
scenes.summary: Apollo loves Hymenaeus, and Hermes steals his cattle and drives them to Coryphasium. Battus betrays the secret for a robe, and Hermes turns him into rock.
scenes.stakes: Battus risks Hermes' anger by breaking his oath; he is turned to stone.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.
Epithets of Poseidon, who is not named in the text.

notable_quotes.reason: Hermes punishes Battus' double-tongued betrayal by turning him into a rock.

analysis.text: The fragments show the catalogue form: genealogies linking heroes to gods and cities, with short myths attached.
The poem survives only in quotations by later scholars and travellers like Pausanias, who used it for local lineages and etymologies.

legacy.text: The story of Hermes stealing Apollo's cattle echoes the Homeric Hymn to Hermes and later retellings.

fun_facts.text: The 'Eoiae' takes its name from the formula 'or like her', which introduced each heroine.

language_notes.text: PONEROS normally means 'bad' in Greek, but the commentator argues Hesiod uses it for 'toilsome' or 'ill-fated', so Heracles is both hard-worked and excellent.
Aias (Ajax) was said to take his name from the eagle (Greek aietos), sent by Zeus as an answer to Heracles' prayer for a brave son for Telamon.
'Lay in the embrace of' is a conventional euphemism for sexual union, here between the god and a mortal woman.
'Earth-holder and Earth-Shaker' are epithets of Poseidon, who is the father of Euphemus by Mecionice; the god is not named.
Minyan Orchomenus is the Boeotian city of the Minyans, a legendary early people; Hyettus the exile settles there.
"Lacedemonian" means a man of Lacedaemon, that is Sparta.
"Befooled with a shape of cloud": Zeus tricked Endymion by giving him a cloud made to look like Hera, so he never possessed her.
"Inspire him with prophecy": the serpents' licking cleansed his ears so he understood birds and other creatures' speech, giving prophetic knowledge.
Melampus' prophetic hearing let him learn from woodworms that the roof beam was rotten, so his warning about the collapsing house won his release.
Phrixus fled on the golden ram toward Colchis; Phineus, a Thracian king, directed him, and for this the gods are said to have blinded Phineus.
Magnesia, the Thessalian region, is explained as named after Magnes; this is an eponym story, a common way Greek tradition explained place names.
Strangles is a disease causing swelling of the throat; here it helps explain why the dogs cannot bark.
"Never yoked" means the cows had never been put under a plough or cart, so they were untamed and unworked.
Hermes disguises himself to test Battus. Disguise as a trial of someone's word is a common motif in Greek stories.
"Double-tongued" means deceitful, saying one thing and doing another; Battus first promised silence and then spoke.
The sentence is awkward: it means the rock is always exposed to frost or heat, so Battus is punished perpetually.

context_notes.text: Fragments here are quotations from later authors such as Pausanias and scholiasts, since the Great Eoiae itself survives only in pieces.
Killing an adulterer in one's own house was an offence requiring exile and purification in early Greek tradition, which explains Hyettus' flight.
Mycene, daughter of Inachus (the river-god of Argos), is the legendary eponym of the city Mycenae.
Oenomaus, king of Pisa, challenged his daughter Hippodamia's suitors to a chariot race and killed each loser, until Pelops defeated him.
Melampus was a legendary Greek seer, said to be the first mortal prophet and physician.
Scylla is the sea monster who haunted the strait opposite Charybdis; Hecate was a goddess of magic and night.
Aeetes was king of Colchis, keeper of the Golden Fleece; Phrixus had fled there on the ram, and married his daughter.
Hermes was the divine trickster and patron of thieves. Stealing Apollo's cattle is his famous exploit, told also in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes.
The route runs from Thessaly south through central Greece into the Peloponnesus; the long journey and the brushwood trick are meant to hide the theft.

literary_notes.text: Alcmene's words define Heracles as a hero whose excellence is inseparable from suffering and labour.
'Famous Iolaus' is a stock descriptive epithet, and the comparison to the Olympians adds heroic idealisation.
Thero's beauty is compared to moonbeams, a typical epic way of praising a woman's radiance.
The list of doomed suitors follows the Eoiae's catalogue form, piling up names to stress Oenomaus' cruelty and the race's repeated deadly outcome.
Endymion, favored by Zeus, is ruined by overreaching desire; the cloud-phantom makes his punishment a mocking parody of his wish.
Hermes' cunning is shown by his neutralising the guard dogs first, before taking any cattle.
Hermes, a notorious deceiver himself, punishes Battus for deceit, and the test he set was itself a trick.
The tale ends by explaining a landmark: a rock exposed to weather is said to be the transformed Battus.
